title: GCGNet: Graph-Consistent Time Series Forecasting
one_liner: Forecast future time series by jointly learning temporal and channel correlations, then refining the prediction to match the true correlation patterns.
lead: Time series forecasting with exogenous variables requires predicting future values of a target metric (like electricity demand) given its past and the future values of related metrics (like weather, price). Most methods model time relationships and channel relationships separately, treating them as two independent problems. GCGNet jointly learns both at once by enforcing that the correlations in its predictions match the correlations in the real data.

problem.h2: Forecasting with both past and future side information
paras: A utility company wants to forecast tomorrow's electricity demand. It has years of past demand data (the endogenous variable). It also knows tomorrow's temperature, time of day, and whether it is a holiday (exogenous variables). Here is why this matters: if tomorrow's temperature is abnormally high, demand will rise; if tomorrow is a holiday, demand will drop. So tomorrow's exogenous values directly affect tomorrow's endogenous target.

A naive approach models temporal relationships (demand today affects demand tomorrow) and channel relationships (temperature correlates with demand) separately, like two independent filters. This misses the joint effect: the way temperature and time-of-day interact depends on the day's baseline demand pattern. In noisy real data, two separate models also train independently on the noise, amplifying errors.

The deeper problem: no mechanism enforces that the joint predictions respect the correlation patterns shown in the real data. The model might predict values that, when analyzed afterward, show impossible patterns (e.g., forecasted electricity demand and temperature that move in ways they never do in reality).

callout.html: Use a graph discriminator to compare correlation patterns between predicted and real data, enforcing that predictions match true relationships.

steps.text: Variational generator produces initial prediction for future values.
Compute which channels move together in both real and predicted data.
Graph discriminator rates how well predicted correlations match real ones.
Graph refiner adjusts forecast values to align with real correlations, because when edges match, individual value errors shrink.
Final prediction respects both temporal order and channel relationships.

paras: The paper's core move is to change how the model learns correlations. Instead of learning temporal patterns and channel patterns separately, it learns them jointly by building a correlation graph (a map showing which pairs of channels move together) from both real and predicted data, then enforcing that the predicted graph matches the real one.

hidden.h2: Graph consistency: matching real and predicted correlation patterns
hidden.name: graph consistency score
paras: The paper measures a quantity called graph consistency: a number that says how similar the correlation patterns are between the real data and the predicted data. Correlation patterns are represented as graphs, where each node is a time-series channel (e.g., demand, temperature, hour-of-day) and each edge connects two channels that move together.

The graph discriminator computes this score by comparing the edges in the real correlation graph against the edges in the predicted correlation graph. If predictions have the same co-movements as the real data, the score is high. If the predicted channels move in ways that never happen in reality, the score is low. The paper uses graphs because they resist noise: a noisy edge still connects the right channels, whereas raw correlation values bounce around with random fluctuations.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger correlation. Mismatches between real and predicted edges penalize the generator, guiding it toward realistic patterns.

reads.html: A graph is just a set of connections between things. In time-series forecasting, connections are correlations (when one channel rises, does another rise with it?). The discriminator checks whether predicted and real channels have the same correlations.

The graph discriminator enforces graph consistency by measuring the divergence between the edge structure of real and generated correlation graphs, making the generator resist noise by penalizing unrealistic correlation patterns.

mechanism.h2: Why jointly learning and enforcing consistency works
paras: A naive forecast model updates its weights by looking only at prediction error: the difference between what it predicted and what actually happened. In noisy data, this signal is weak and unreliable. The model makes two mistakes independently in its time branch and channel branch, and the errors compound.

GCGNet adds a second signal: the graph discriminator. During training, the generator produces a forecast; the discriminator then checks whether the correlations implied by that forecast match the real data's correlations. If they do not, the discriminator sends back a penalty. This penalty does not depend on whether the individual predicted values are right or wrong—it depends only on whether the joint patterns are plausible. In noisy data, individual values bounce around, but correlation patterns are stable (demand and temperature correlate because of fundamental physics, not randomness). So the discriminator gives a clean, stable signal that guides the generator away from learning noise and toward learning true relationships.

The graph refiner then polishes the forecast in a second pass. It adjusts the prediction values to be both accurate and consistent with the enforced correlations, preventing the prediction from drifting or degrading during this alignment process.

stages.s: Extract real correlation graph from data
Extract predicted correlation graph from forecast
Graph refiner aligns forecast with real correlations

math.words: The total loss is: prediction error plus a weight times graph mismatch. Graph mismatch is computed as the sum of differences between real and predicted correlation edges across all channel pairs.
symbols: how far the forecast is from true values
how much to penalize graph mismatch
correlation strength between two channels in real data (0 to 1)
correlation strength between the same two channels in predicted data (0 to 1)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we forecast 3 channels: Demand, Temperature, Holiday-Flag.
Real data correlations: Demand-Temperature = 0.8 (strong), Demand-Holiday = 0.6 (medium), Temperature-Holiday = 0.1 (weak).
Predicted correlations: Demand-Temperature = 0.9 (too strong), Demand-Holiday = 0.3 (too weak), Temperature-Holiday = 0.1 (correct).
The model learns that predicting the right correlation patterns (even at a small overall cost) matters as much as predicting the exact values, because the mismatch penalty is large.

math.note: The graph discriminator measures edge mismatches to enforce that predicted time-series correlations match real patterns, giving a stable training signal in noisy data.

charts.title: Separate time and channel models
charts.note: Treating temporal and channel correlations independently works well for clean datasets but fails on noisy real-world scenarios.

charts.title: GCGNet with graph consistency
charts.note: Enforcing graph consistency stabilizes predictions across different noise levels and data types, improving accuracy on all tasks.

items.html: If lambda is too high, the model focuses so hard on matching correlation patterns that it ignores prediction accuracy. A forecast could have perfect correlations but be off by years of values.

items.b: Real data has no clear correlations.
items.html: If channels are truly independent (e.g., demand and unrelated random noise), the model has nothing to enforce. It will predict poorly because the graph signal is uninformative.

If correlations change over time (e.g., before and after a policy change), the real correlation graph from historical data does not match the future correlation structure. Predictions will be misaligned with new reality.
Tune lambda using a validation set. Retrain the correlation model on recent data. Use graph methods that handle missing edges and short time windows.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny time-series forecasting task: generate synthetic data with two channels (e.g., hourly temperature and humidity) that always correlate strongly. Add noise to the data. Train a naive model that predicts independently for each channel. Train GCGNet with graph consistency. Compare the forecasts: the naive model's predictions should show channel patterns that contradict the data (temperature rises while humidity falls), while GCGNet's predictions should preserve the real correlation (when temperature rises, humidity rises).
demo.metric_eq: correlation_fidelity = (predicted_correlation - real_correlation)^2 summed over all channel pairs
demo.closing: GCGNet's forecasts must show the same correlation structure as real data, even on noisy examples where individual values differ from ground truth.
